History:
• 35-year-old male lawyer presents with intermittent frontal headaches, episodic palpitations, shortness of breath, bilateral arm tingling, diminished appetite, ~5 lb unintentional weight loss, subjective heat intolerance, and decreased libido.  
• Symptom onset: began shortly after changing to current job (exact date not specified; “same amount of time” for all symptoms).  
• Temporal pattern: headaches and other episodes occur mainly during work hours while on computer or in meetings; rarely during commute or exercise. Each symptom tends to occur separately rather than simultaneously.  
• Headache characteristics: frontal, severe, non-radiating, occur at work; associated with mild nausea; no prior headache history.  
• Palpitations: felt “once a day, maybe more,” occasionally when entering the elevator or sitting at desk.  
• Shortness of breath: episodic while seated at desk; not with exercise.  
• Tingling: quick “pricking” sensation in both arms; no leg involvement.  
• Stress level: rates work stress 7–8/10.  
• No identified precipitants other than work; no relieving measures reported.

Past Medical History:
• “Hyperthyroidism” (patient report).  
• Medications: Thyroxine – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• Allergies: Not recorded.  
• Social: Alcohol – couple of glasses of wine once weekly; non-smoker; denies recreational drug use.  
• Family history, surgical history, immunizations: Not recorded.

Physical Examination:
• Tele-visit; no vitals or physical findings obtained.  
• Mental status: alert, oriented, able to converse.  
• No other exam data recorded.

Impression:
Intermittent frontal headaches with autonomic and constitutional symptoms in a patient on thyroxine. Differential considerations:  
1. Possible iatrogenic hyperthyroidism from thyroxine (heat intolerance, weight loss, palpitations).  
2. Stress-related/anxiety episodes with tension-type headaches (symptoms cluster during high-stress work periods).  
3. Primary headache disorder (tension or migraine) exacerbated by screen work.  
(Note: All consistent with transcript.)

Management Plan:
• Arrange in-person clinic appointment for full examination (cardiac and respiratory auscultation).  
• Order blood tests, including thyroid function tests, at that visit.  
• No new medications prescribed during tele-visit; defer treatment decisions until after physical exam and labs.  
• Patient instructed to book appointment via clinic app; clinician will forward today’s history to in-clinic team.  
• Address stress management and workplace ergonomics at follow-up as appropriate.

Patient Summary:
35-year-old man with new job-related onset of severe frontal headaches and autonomic symptoms; thyroid dysfunction or stress-related etiology suspected. Will be seen in clinic for examination and thyroid labs before further management.

Key Takeaways:
• Book an in-person appointment promptly for exam and blood work.  
• Continue current thyroxine until reviewed; do not adjust dose on your own.  
• Seek urgent care if severe chest pain, persistent shortness of breath, or worsening neurological signs occur.

Next Steps:
• In-clinic vitals and focused neuro/cardiopulmonary exam.  
• Thyroid panel (TSH, free T4/T3); consider CBC, electrolytes, B12 if paresthesia persists.  
• Reassess symptoms and medication needs after results; consider stress-reduction strategies or headache prophylaxis depending on findings.
